title: Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence
before: A conversation about inviting participation honestly: naming what people can shape and showing how their input reached a decision.

turns.text: This course is Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence. It’s about the moment before we invite anyone to participate, whether that’s community members, people using services, or our own colleagues. The central question is simple and sometimes uncomfortable: what can people actually shape? An honest invitation starts with that answer.

The opening case puts you on the receiving end. Imagine being asked to help shape an onboarding guide after its content has already been settled. What can your contribution still change? A review after a decision can be useful, but it shouldn’t be described as shared design of a choice that’s already closed.

The course gives us language for this. Informing explains. Seeking input asks for a response. Shared design involves people in shaping alternatives. Shared decision-making includes actual authority. Each can be appropriate when it’s named accurately. What doesn’t work is letting attendance, an advisory title, or a distribution list stand in for the depth of the relationship.

In the first practice situation, a service team is comparing two ways to explain a response process, and both can still change. You’ll decide which invitation best supports meaningful input. It’s worth noticing what the course says about asking only after decisions are fixed: it can preserve existing power while creating the appearance of shared design.

Then there’s who gets invited. A familiar partner list may not include the range of people affected, and some invited people may not be able to use the response route. The course is careful that no one person should stand for everyone who shares an identity or a service connection. And family input shouldn’t automatically replace the person’s own voice.

Participation also has costs. Time, travel, communication support, and preparation all affect who can take part, and some of those burdens are hard to see from inside an office. The course asks us to discuss feasible arrangements through the appropriate process, without promising payment or resources we don’t have authority to offer, and without assuming willingness means there’s no cost.

The second practice situation comes back to the onboarding guide. It’s final, but staff are still being invited to help design it. You’ll choose the most honest response. I think many of us have been on one side or the other of that kind of invitation, so it’s a useful one to sit with for a minute.

After people contribute, the work isn’t finished. The course asks us to show how input changed an option, identified a concern, or supported a reason for keeping part of the design. A thank-you alone doesn’t explain influence. And when a suggestion isn’t adopted, we can explain why without implying that someone’s experience was invalid.

The third situation is about the report-back. One participant says the revised message reflects their concern, and another hasn’t replied. Those are different facts. You’ll decide how the account should describe the result. The broader point is that silence isn’t approval, and one positive comment isn’t a population outcome.

Near the end, you’ll privately rewrite a practice message that says, help us design the new guide, the final version has already been approved. The task is to name the actual opportunity and what can still change. If no choice is open, you’d describe information sharing or a later review honestly instead of promising shared design.

As you go, think of an invitation you’ve sent or received at work, to a community group, a team, or a review. What could participants actually influence, and did the invitation say so? Bring that situation with you. When the promise matches the opportunity, people can decide for themselves how to spend their time and knowledge.

guidance.title: Naming the depth accurately
guidance.text: Each level of participation can be the right one. Sometimes the honest choice is simply to inform people well, because the decision is made and they deserve a clear explanation. The problem comes when the label promises more than the arrangement offers. Before an invitation goes out, try naming the level in plain words and checking it against who actually holds the decision.

guidance.title: Matching the promise to the opportunity
guidance.text: Think of an engagement effort you’re part of, with community members or colleagues. Could you explain to a participant what is still open, who decides, and how their input will be considered? If any part of that answer is uncertain, who could clarify it before the invitation goes out? What would an honest report-back look like afterward?
